figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Comparison of different agent-memory operating regimes. Generative memory relies on LLM-generated abstractions, while raw retrieval searches unstructured traces and may miss distributed evidence. Zero-Mem builds relational and temporal memory structures and performs all memory operations with zero LLM calls or tokens; only final QA invokes an LLM.
figures.headline: Zero-Mem performs every memory operation with zero LLM calls, while generative memory relies on LLM-generated abstractions.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Overview of Zero-Mem. Original interaction traces are organized into a provenance-preserving entity–context graph and temporal hierarchy without generative abstraction. Query-conditioned routing weights the two views, whose retrieved evidence is fused and completed with relational bridges and local neighbors. Deterministic calibration filters and ranks the evidence and checks the reader output. All memory operations are token-free; the final-QA reader is the only LLM call.
figures.headline: Zero-Mem routes each query across a graph view and a hierarchy view, and only the final reader calls an LLM.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Ablation study on HotpotQA with 56K-token contexts and GPT-4o-mini. The full model outperforms both single-view variants, demonstrating the complementarity of graph-based relational retrieval and hierarchical contextual retrieval. Evidence closure and calibration provide further gains on both F1 and BLEU-1.
figures.headline: Removing either the graph view or the hierarchy view lowers HotpotQA F1 below the full model's 72.07.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 reports ablation results on HotpotQA with 56K-token contexts and GPT-4o-mini.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Effect of the retrieval budget on LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini. Performance improves markedly from top-1 to top-5, reaches its best average at top-10, and remains stable under larger budgets. We use top-5 in the main experiments to match the retrieval setting of all baselines.
figures.headline: Average F1 on LoCoMo rises from 52.59 at top-1 to 59.15 at top-5, then remains stable at larger budgets.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 examines the sensitivity of Zero-Mem to the retrieval budget, defined as the maximum number of primary candidates retained in $M(q)$ before evidence closure.

abstract: LLM agents need memory to act consistently over long interactions, yet many systems use additional LLM calls to operate that memory. Generating intermediate records and mediating their retrieval adds recurring token and time costs, while omitted or merged details can obscure the original evidence. We ask whether structured memory access requires generation at all. Zero-Mem introduces zero-token memory operations: no step outside final question answering invokes an LLM or consumes LLM input or output tokens; encoder computation is accounted for separately. Zero-Mem preserves original interaction traces as its source of record. It organizes the traces in two complementary ways. An entity–context graph exposes connections across interactions, while a temporal hierarchy preserves conversational locality and session state. For each query, Zero-Mem weighs the two views, retrieves from both, and follows their structure to recover supporting relations or surrounding context. Deterministic calibration first discards conflicting evidence and then keeps the reader’s answer grounded in the retrieved traces. Only the final-QA reader invokes an LLM. Across long-memory and long-context question-answering benchmarks, Zero-Mem achieves competitive performance while eliminating LLM calls and LLM-token consumption from memory operations. With the same final-QA reader and context budget, it reduces memory-operation time cost by 57.6% relative to the fastest compared baseline. Ablations support the contribution of the two views and their query-dependent coordination. Overall, the results show that structured agent memory need not generate an intermediate representation of the past. After peer review, the code and implementation details will be available at https://github.com/TheMoon0815/Zero-mem.

sections.body: LLM agent memory systems often call an LLM to summarize, index, or link memory records. This adds token and time costs and can obscure the original evidence. The section asks whether structured memory access needs generation at all. It defines zero-token memory operations, in which no step outside final question answering invokes an LLM or consumes LLM tokens. Zero-Mem keeps original interaction traces as the source of record, organizes them into an entity–context graph and a temporal hierarchy, and calls an LLM only for final answering. The section reports competitive benchmark performance and a 57.6% reduction in memory-operation latency relative to the most time-efficient baseline.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Agent memory systems often call an LLM for memory operations, and this work asks whether structured access needs generation.

sections.body: The section surveys agent-memory systems. Zep builds a temporally aware knowledge graph. Mem0 extracts and updates memories through LLM tool calls. A-Mem builds linked memory notes with keywords and tags. MemoryOS uses short-term, mid-term, and long-term storage. GAM combines lightweight offline memory with online research, at higher query-time cost. LightMem and SimpleMem reduce token consumption. The section states that these systems improve memory efficiency, while many retain generative processing within the memory lifecycle. It reports no experiments.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior systems such as Zep, Mem0, and LightMem reduce memory cost, but many keep generative steps in the memory lifecycle.

sections.body:
The section defines the setting formally. An agent history is a sequence of trace units. Each unit may contain user messages, assistant responses or actions, tool observations, timestamps, speakers, and session metadata. Given a query, a memory function returns an evidence set from the history. A reader LLM then produces the answer from that evidence. Zero-Mem instantiates the memory function through non-generative construction, organization, retrieval, routing, and calibration.

$$
R(q)=\operatorname{Memory}(q,\mathcal{H}).
$$
sections.heading: Preliminaries
sections.headline: Memory is formalized as a function returning evidence from the history, which a reader model then uses to answer.

sections.body: Zero-Mem keeps each derived unit tied to its original text and source identifier. The graph view links entities detected by a named entity recognition model to context units, with edge weights set by normalized occurrence frequency, and connects adjacent units. The hierarchy view groups traces into turns, windows, episodes, and local spans. Routing assigns the graph view or the hierarchy view as the primary view, based on query structure. Evidence closure adds graph-ranked context and neighboring turns. Deterministic calibration filters candidates by provenance and boundary constraints, ranks them, and checks the reader's answer without another model call.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Zero-Mem selects evidence from raw traces using a graph view, a hierarchy view, routing, closure, and deterministic calibration.

sections.body: On LoCoMo, Zero-Mem improves average F1 over GAM by 5.40 with GPT-4o-mini and by 4.87 with Qwen2.5-14B. On HotpotQA, it gives an average improvement of 5.52 points over the strongest baseline across context lengths. In the efficiency comparison, Zero-Mem uses zero tokens for memory operations, while LightMem, the most token-efficient baseline, consumes more than 0.87 million tokens. Zero-Mem requires 334.77 seconds in total and 0.22 seconds per query. The ablation on HotpotQA at 56K tokens gives 72.07 F1 for the full model, 62.50 with the graph view alone, and 54.88 with the hierarchy view alone. The authors state that zero-token operation does not imply zero computation.
sections.heading: Experiment
sections.headline: Zero-Mem scores highest on HotpotQA and on LoCoMo averages, while cutting memory-operation time 57.6% versus LightMem.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the zero-token regime, in which every operation outside final question answering uses no LLM calls or tokens. Zero-Mem preserves raw traces and retrieves evidence through relational and temporally ordered views. The authors report competitive performance on conversational memory and long-context multi-hop reasoning. Ablations confirm the complementarity of the two views. With the same final-QA reader and context budget, Zero-Mem removes memory-operation token consumption and reduces latency by 57.6% relative to the most time-efficient baseline. The authors conclude that provenance-preserving evidence selection is a practical alternative to generative memory pipelines.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Structured agent memory can work without generated intermediate representations, with competitive performance and no memory-operation token cost.
